abstract: Global climate change and shrinking freshwater supplies threaten agricultural sustainability. A major translational bottleneck exists: drought-tolerant genotypes developed in labs often fail in open-field conditions due to phenotypic mismatch. Traditional single-gene approaches and static lab tests overlook genotype-by-environment (G × E) interactions, hormonal tradeoffs (involving Abscisic Acid, Jasmonic Acid, Brassinosteroids, and Melatonin), and artificial effects of pots. This review presents an integrated quantitative selection framework to bridge lab and field results. In this review, we propose a conceptual three-stage Predictive Translational Workflow designed to bridge lab and field outcomes by integrating multi-omics envirotyping with advanced mixed models like (G × E)-BLUP and MegaLMM. These methods group complex transcriptomic and metabolomic data into functional networks, filtering out lab artifacts and pinpointing core regulatory nodes stable in real climates. Finally, we show how this pipeline enables precise CRISPR/Cas9 editing of native promoters, reducing agronomic yield penalties in normal conditions and offering a streamlined, non-GMO path to field-resilient crops.
